course_title: Cisco Certified Internetwork Expert (CCIE) Enterprise Infrastructure
chapter_title: Introduction to VPN Concepts and IPsec Fundamentals
chapter_summary:
Virtual Private Networks (VPNs) are foundational to secure communication over untrusted networks, particularly the internet. At their core, VPNs create a secure, encrypted "tunnel" between two or more points, making a public network behave like a private one. This allows organizations to extend their private network securely across vast geographical distances, connecting branch offices, remote workers, or cloud resources as if they were directly connected to the corporate LAN. The primary benefits of VPNs include enhanced security through encryption and authentication, cost savings by leveraging public internet infrastructure instead of dedicated private lines, and increased flexibility for remote work and distributed operations. We primarily categorize VPNs into two main types: site-to-site VPNs, which connect entire networks (e.g., a branch office to a headquarters), and remote access VPNs, which allow individual users to securely connect to a corporate network from anywhere.

The Internet Protocol Security (IPsec) suite is the most widely adopted framework for implementing VPNs, especially site-to-site and some remote access scenarios. IPsec operates at the network layer (Layer 3) of the OSI model, providing robust security services directly to IP traffic. Its comprehensive architecture ensures confidentiality, integrity, authenticity, and anti-replay protection. Confidentiality is achieved through encryption, scrambling the data so only authorized parties can read it. Integrity ensures that the data has not been tampered with in transit. Authenticity verifies the identity of the communicating parties, preventing unauthorized access. Anti-replay protection guards against an attacker intercepting and retransmitting old packets to disrupt services or gain unauthorized access. Understanding IPsec is critical for any network expert.

IPsec is not a single protocol but a suite of protocols working together. The two main protocols within IPsec are Authentication Header (AH) and Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP). AH provides connectionless integrity, data origin authentication, and an optional anti-replay service, but it does not provide confidentiality (encryption). It authenticates the entire IP packet, including the IP header. ESP, on the other hand, provides confidentiality (encryption), limited traffic flow confidentiality, and connectionless integrity, data origin authentication, and an anti-replay service. ESP encrypts the IP payload and optionally authenticates the entire ESP packet (including the ESP header and payload). Due to its encryption capabilities, ESP is far more commonly used than AH in modern VPN deployments. Both AH and ESP can operate in two modes: Transport mode and Tunnel mode. In Transport mode, the IPsec header is inserted between the original IP header and the IP payload, protecting only the payload. This mode is typically used for host-to-host communication. In Tunnel mode, which is standard for VPNs, the entire original IP packet is encapsulated with a new IP header, protecting the original IP header and payload. This is essential for site-to-site VPNs where traffic from an internal network needs to be securely tunneled across an external network.

Key to establishing an IPsec VPN is the Internet Key Exchange (IKE) protocol, which handles the negotiation and management of Security Associations (SAs). SAs are the core building blocks of IPsec; they are simplex (one-way) logical connections that define the parameters for secure communication, including cryptographic algorithms, keys, and lifetimes. IKE itself operates in two phases. IKE Phase 1, also known as the ISAKMP (Internet Security Association and Key Management Protocol) SA, establishes a secure, authenticated channel between two IPsec peers. This phase is responsible for authenticating the peers (using pre-shared keys or digital certificates) and establishing a secure tunnel for IKE messages. It negotiates parameters like encryption algorithm (e.g., AES), hashing algorithm (e.g., SHA256), authentication method, Diffie-Hellman group for key exchange, and the lifetime of the Phase 1 SA. A common mistake here is mismatched Phase 1 parameters between peers, leading to negotiation failures. Always ensure that encryption, hashing, authentication, and DH group are identical on both sides.

Once the IKE Phase 1 SA is established, IKE Phase 2 begins. In this phase, the peers use the secure channel established in Phase 1 to negotiate the IPsec SAs that will protect the actual user data traffic. Phase 2 defines the specific parameters for data encryption and authentication, including the IPsec protocol (AH or ESP), encryption algorithm (e.g., AES-256), hashing algorithm (e.g., SHA384), and the lifetime of the IPsec SA. It also defines the "proxy identities" or "interesting traffic" – the specific traffic (source/destination IP addresses, ports, protocols) that will be protected by the IPsec tunnel. A crucial aspect of Phase 2 is Perfect Forward Secrecy (PFS), an optional feature that ensures if a single session key is compromised, it doesn't compromise past or future session keys. PFS is achieved by performing a new Diffie-Hellman exchange for each Phase 2 negotiation, generating a unique key for each IPsec SA. While it adds overhead, PFS is highly recommended for robust security.

IKEv1 and IKEv2 are two versions of the Internet Key Exchange protocol. IKEv1, the older standard, uses a more complex negotiation process with "main mode" and "aggressive mode" for Phase 1. Main mode is more secure as it protects peer identities, while aggressive mode is faster but reveals identities. IKEv2, defined in RFC 4306, is a significant improvement offering several advantages: it's simpler and more efficient (fewer messages exchanged), supports MOBIKE (Mobility and Multihoming Protocol for IKEv2) for seamless VPN re-establishment when IP addresses change, has built-in support for NAT traversal, and offers enhanced reliability and anti-DoS features. For new deployments, IKEv2 is generally preferred due to its superior security, efficiency, and flexibility. When troubleshooting, remember that IKEv1 and IKEv2 are incompatible; both peers must be configured to use the same IKE version. Misconfigured crypto access lists (ACLs) defining interesting traffic are another common pitfall, preventing traffic from being encrypted and sent over the tunnel. Always verify that your ACLs correctly match the traffic intended for the VPN.

screens.title: Introduction to VPNs and IPsec Fundamentals
screens.subtitle: How enterprises establish secure tunnels across untrusted networks

narration.text: Today you will learn what a Virtual Private Network is and why IPsec is the dominant way to build secure, scalable tunnels across the public internet. A VPN makes an untrusted network behave like a private link by encrypting and authenticating traffic so remote offices, cloud resources, and mobile users can exchange data as if they were on the corporate LAN. IPsec works at the IP layer and combines protocols—AH and ESP—with a key-management protocol, IKE, to deliver confidentiality, integrity, authentication, and anti-replay protection. You will also see how IKE Phase 1 and Phase 2 form the foundation of trust, and why mismatched parameters are the most common cause of tunnel failure. As we progress you will get concrete examples: a site-to-site tunnel carrying multiple subnets, the role of ESP for encryption, and a short configuration snippet to identify Phase 1 and Phase 2 parameters. Keep an eye out for two common misconfigurations: mismatched crypto parameters and incorrect proxy access lists. By the end you should be able to read an IPsec configuration, identify SAs and transforms, and explain why IKEv2 is generally preferred for new deployments.

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: VPNs create encrypted tunnels; IPsec provides the protocols and key exchange to protect IP traffic with AH/ESP and IKE phases.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: Skills you'll gain and why they matter

narration.text: These objectives frame practical, testable skills you will develop. First, you will explain core VPN principles and the benefits they deliver in enterprise environments: secure connectivity, cost efficiency, and support for distributed work. Second, you will differentiate common VPN types: site-to-site tunnels that connect networks and remote access VPNs for individual users. Third, you will describe the architecture and phases of IPsec and IKE, including the separate roles of Phase 1 and Phase 2. Fourth, you will identify Security Association components and explain how IPsec achieves confidentiality, integrity, authenticity, and anti-replay protection. Each objective supports practical troubleshooting: when you can map a misconfiguration to an IKE phase, you can resolve failed tunnels faster. As you study, apply each objective to the included configuration analysis so you can identify Phase 1 and Phase 2 parameters and reason about negotiation failures.

screens.title: What is a VPN?
screens.subtitle: Definition, benefits, and primary enterprise use cases

narration.text: A Virtual Private Network is a method for creating a secure, encrypted connection across an untrusted network so resources can communicate as if they were on the same private LAN. In practice this means building a tunnel that encrypts traffic between peers and authenticates the endpoints. The benefits are practical: encryption protects sensitive data in transit, authentication prevents unauthorized peers from joining, and using the public internet reduces the need for expensive private lines. Common enterprise use cases include site-to-site VPNs that connect branch offices to headquarters and remote access VPNs that let individual employees work securely from home or while traveling. A misconception to avoid is thinking a VPN alone solves all security concerns; it protects the transport but does not replace host hardening, access control, or application-layer protections. For example, a site-to-site tunnel may encrypt traffic between offices, but inside the tunnel you still need careful ACLs and segmentation. Concrete example: a branch office routing two internal subnets over an IPsec tunnel to HQ, where remote services are accessed without exposing those subnets to the public internet. Your takeaway is that VPNs are a transport security tool—powerful and essential—but they must be combined with broader security controls.

keyIdea.title: VPN takeaway
keyIdea.text: VPNs secure transport and extend networks, but they are one piece of a multi-layer security design.

content.html:
Chapter 6.1›What is a VPN?
Definition
A VPN is an encrypted tunnel over a public network that makes remote resources appear as part of a private network.
Benefits
  • Confidentiality and authentication for traffic over untrusted networks.
  • Cost savings by using the internet instead of leased lines.
  • Flexible remote work and distributed operations.
Key Takeaway

Treat the VPN as transport security; combine it with access control and segmentation inside the tunnel.

Primary types
Site-to-site: Connects entire networks, commonly used for branch-to-headquarters links.
Remote access: Individual users connect into the corporate network from anywhere.
Analogy
Think of a VPN as a private, locked hallway built through a public building; it prevents eavesdroppers from seeing who passes through.

screens.title: What IPsec Provides
screens.subtitle: Confidentiality, integrity, authenticity, and anti-replay protection

narration.text: IPsec is a protocol suite that secures IP traffic at the network layer. Its goals are fourfold: confidentiality so only authorized parties can read payloads, integrity to detect tampering, authenticity to confirm the identity of peers, and anti-replay protection to prevent capture-and-replay attacks. These services are realized by combining AH and ESP with cryptographic keys negotiated by IKE. AH offers integrity and authentication for the IP packet but does not encrypt payloads, so it does not provide confidentiality. ESP, by contrast, provides confidentiality through encryption and also supports integrity and authentication, making it the common choice for VPNs. Anti-replay is implemented with sequence numbers and window checks to discard duplicated or replayed packets. An important architectural note: IPsec operates at Layer 3, which means it protects all IP traffic independent of higher-layer protocols. That is a strength because it is protocol-agnostic, but it also means IPsec does not replace higher-layer controls like application authentication. A common misconception is to assume AH and ESP are mutually exclusive: they can be combined in some deployments, but ESP alone typically meets confidentiality and integrity needs for VPNs. Your takeaway: understand each security service and map it to AH or ESP so you can design the right protection for a given use case.

keyIdea.title: IPsec services
keyIdea.text: AH = integrity/authentication; ESP = encryption plus integrity; sequence checks provide anti-replay.

content.html:
IPsec›What IPsec Provides
Security services
  • Confidentiality: payload encryption so only authorized peers read the data.
  • Integrity: hashing ensures packets were not altered in transit.
  • Authenticity: verifies the identity of the sending peer before accepting traffic.
  • Anti-replay: sequence numbers and windows discard replayed packets.
Protocol roles
AH
Integrity, authentication, optional anti-replay; no encryption.
ESP
Encryption for confidentiality plus integrity and authentication features; most common for VPNs.
Common misconception

ESP alone usually satisfies confidentiality and integrity needs; AH is rarely used for modern VPNs because it lacks encryption.

Why Layer 3 matters
IPsec protects IP traffic regardless of applications, making it broad but also requiring layered controls.
Key Takeaway
Map each security requirement to AH or ESP and use ESP for encrypted VPN traffic.

screens.title: AH vs ESP and Modes
screens.subtitle: Protocol differences and Transport vs Tunnel modes

narration.text: AH and ESP are the two main IPsec protocols, but they serve different purposes and are applied in different modes. Authentication Header provides integrity and data origin authentication for packets and can include anti-replay, but it does not encrypt payloads. Encapsulating Security Payload provides encryption for confidentiality plus optional authentication and anti-replay; this makes ESP the practical default for VPNs. Both AH and ESP can operate in transport mode or tunnel mode. In Transport mode, the IPsec header is placed between the original IP header and the payload, protecting only the payload and leaving the IP header intact. Transport mode is useful for host-to-host scenarios where only payload protection is needed. In Tunnel mode, the entire original IP packet is encapsulated and a new outer IP header is added, protecting both the original header and payload; this is the common choice for site-to-site VPNs because it hides internal addressing. A frequent mistake is choosing transport mode for a site-to-site design where tunnel mode is required. Another common confusion is assuming AH provides privacy; it does not. Concrete example: a remote client using ESP in tunnel mode to send traffic from a private IP to a data center subnet so the entire original packet, including internal IPs, is protected. Closing question: when would you prefer transport mode over tunnel mode and why?

keyIdea.title: Mode decision
keyIdea.text: Use transport mode for host-to-host payload protection; use tunnel mode for network-to-network privacy and address hiding.

content.html:
Core Concept›AH vs ESP & Modes
Protocol comparison
AH
Integrity, authentication, optional anti-replay; no encryption.
ESP
Encryption plus integrity and authentication; most widely used for VPNs.
Modes
Transport mode
Protects only the payload; used for host-to-host encryption.
Tunnel mode
Encapsulates the full original packet with a new header; used for site-to-site VPNs.
Concrete example
A VPN between two sites uses ESP in tunnel mode so internal IP addresses remain private and the entire packet is encrypted across the internet.
Common mistake

Choosing transport mode for a site-to-site deployment will fail to protect the original IP header and may expose internal addressing.

Key Takeaway
ESP + Tunnel mode = standard site-to-site VPN setup for confidentiality and header protection.

screens.title: Security Associations (SAs)
screens.subtitle: What an SA is and which parameters it defines

narration.text: A Security Association is the fundamental contract that defines how two peers will secure traffic in one direction. SAs are simplex, meaning you need an SA for each direction of traffic. Each SA contains the cryptographic algorithms, keys, and lifetimes that govern encryption and integrity checks: the encryption algorithm and key (for confidentiality), the hashing algorithm used for integrity, the authentication method, the Diffie-Hellman group if used for key exchanges, and the SA lifetime. IKE negotiates these SAs so both peers have matching parameters. A common source of failure is a mismatch in any one of these parameters; even a different hash algorithm will prevent the SA from forming. Another part of the SA is the scope: Phase 2 negotiation also defines the proxy identities or ACLs that specify the interesting traffic to be protected. In practice, reading an SA involves checking the transform set, the mode (tunnel or transport), and whether PFS is enabled. Concrete example: an SA with AES-256 and SHA-256-HMAC for ESP in tunnel mode with a 3600-second lifetime. Misconception to avoid: thinking an SA is a single bi-directional object—remember it is simplex, so expect two entries for symmetric communication. Takeaway: SAs are the atomic units of policy and key material for IPsec tunnels.

keyIdea.title: SA essentials
keyIdea.text: An SA specifies algorithms, keys, lifetimes, and traffic scope; it is simplex and must match on both peers.

content.html:
Core Concept›Security Associations
SA definition
A simplex contract listing encryption, integrity, keys, and lifetime that two peers agree on to protect traffic in one direction.
Common parameters
  • Encryption algorithm and key (e.g., AES-256).
  • Hashing algorithm for integrity (e.g., SHA-256 or SHA-384).
  • Authentication method and Diffie-Hellman group for key exchange.
  • SA lifetime and replay window settings.
Misconception

An SA is not bi-directional by default. Expect two SAs for bidirectional traffic unless a combined mechanism is used.

Concrete example
ESP with AES-256 and SHA-256-HMAC, tunnel mode, SA lifetime 3600 seconds, PFS enabled with DH group 14.
Check your understanding
When you inspect a peer's SA list, verify algorithms, lifetimes, and whether the SA is simplex or part of a pair.

screens.title: IKE Phase 1 — Establishing the Secure Channel
screens.subtitle: Authentication, DH exchange, and the ISAKMP SA

narration.text: IKE Phase 1 sets up a secure, authenticated channel between two IPsec peers and is often called the ISAKMP SA. During this phase peers authenticate each other—commonly with pre-shared keys or digital certificates—negotiate encryption and hashing algorithms, choose a Diffie-Hellman group for the initial key exchange, and agree upon an SA lifetime. The result is a protected channel for subsequent IKE messages. An important detail: IKEv1 supports modes called main and aggressive. Main mode protects identities and is preferred for security, while aggressive mode is faster but reveals identities, so it is less secure. A frequent troubleshooting point is mismatched Phase 1 parameters: if parties propose different encryption, hash, or DH groups, negotiation fails. This often manifests as an inability to establish any SAs, because Phase 2 relies on the Phase 1 channel. Concrete example: a Phase 1 policy that specifies AES-256 encryption, SHA-384 hashing, pre-shared authentication, DH group 14, and a 86400-second lifetime establishes a durable, authenticated IKE channel. Misconception check: Phase 1 is not where user data is protected; it only secures the keying channel to negotiate Phase 2 SAs.

keyIdea.title: Phase 1 success
keyIdea.text: Phase 1 authenticates peers and creates an encrypted channel for later IPsec SA negotiations; parameter parity is critical.

content.html:
Process›IKE Phase 1
Phase 1 goals
Authenticate peers, negotiate encryption/hash/DH group, and establish the ISAKMP SA for a secure messaging channel.
Typical parameters
  • Encryption (e.g., AES-256)
  • Hash (e.g., SHA-384)
  • Authentication method (pre-shared key or certificates)
  • Diffie-Hellman group and lifetime
Troubleshooting

Mismatched Phase 1 policies often manifest as failures to establish any IPsec SAs. Verify encryption, hash, auth, and DH group first.

Concrete policy
Policy example: AES-256, SHA-384, pre-shared auth, group 14, lifetime 86400 seconds.
Key Takeaway
Phase 1 builds the secure channel for IKE. If it fails, Phase 2 cannot proceed.

screens.title: IKE Phase 2 — Negotiating IPsec SAs and PFS
screens.subtitle: Transform sets, proxy identities, and Perfect Forward Secrecy

narration.text: Once Phase 1 has created a secure channel, IKE Phase 2 negotiates the IPsec Security Associations that directly protect user data. Phase 2 defines the IPsec protocol (AH or ESP), the encryption and hashing algorithms for the IPsec SA, the SA lifetime, and the proxy identities or ACLs that represent the interesting traffic to be tunneled. Perfect Forward Secrecy is an optional, but recommended, feature in Phase 2 that requires a fresh Diffie-Hellman exchange for each SA so compromise of one session key does not reveal past or future keys. While PFS increases C P U and message overhead, it dramatically improves long-term confidentiality. A concrete scenario: two peers negotiate ESP with AES-256 and SHA-256-HMAC in tunnel mode, and they also request PFS with DH group 14; this generates unique session keys for each SA. A common error is omitting matching proxy identities or misconfiguring crypto ACLs so that traffic intended for the tunnel is not considered interesting and therefore not protected. Misconception: PFS is optional but is not a silver bullet—proper key management and secure authentication remain essential. Takeaway: Phase 2 translates policy into material SAs and PFS enhances forward secrecy at the cost of extra exchanges.

keyIdea.title: Phase 2 role
keyIdea.text: Phase 2 creates the IPsec SAs and can use PFS to ensure session keys are independent across negotiations.

content.html:
Process›IKE Phase 2
Phase 2 responsibilities
Negotiate IPsec SAs: choose ESP or AH, set encryption and hash for the data channel, set SA lifetime, and define proxy identities for interesting traffic.
Perfect Forward Secrecy
PFS forces a new Diffie-Hellman exchange to create unique keys for each SA so compromising one key does not affect others.
Practical note

Enable PFS when you require strong forward secrecy; ensure both peers are configured with the same DH group to avoid negotiation failures.

Example SA
ESP: AES-256, SHA-256-HMAC, tunnel mode, PFS group 14, lifetime 3600s; ACLs define the protected source/destination subnets.
Check your understanding
If an SA fails to form for expected traffic, verify proxy identities and whether PFS settings match on both peers.

screens.title: IKEv1 vs IKEv2
screens.subtitle: Advantages of IKEv2 and compatibility considerations

narration.text: IKEv1 and IKEv2 are distinct versions of the Internet Key Exchange protocol with different negotiation models. IKEv1 introduced main and aggressive modes for Phase 1; main mode is more secure because it protects peer identities, whereas aggressive mode is faster but exposes identities. IKEv2 simplifies and streamlines the negotiation flow, reducing message exchanges, improving reliability, and adding features such as MOBIKE for mobility and multihoming. IKEv2 also has better built-in NAT traversal support and stronger resistance to certain denial-of-service conditions. For new deployments, IKEv2 is generally preferred for its efficiency and feature set. However, peers must use the same IKE version; IKEv1 and IKEv2 are incompatible, so mixed-version environments require appropriate peer configuration or gateways that support both. When troubleshooting, confirm the IKE version match in addition to matching crypto parameters. A common operational pitfall is assuming that IKEv2 will automatically replace IKEv1 without checking compatibility with legacy peers or with third-party VPN appliances. Concrete example: enabling IKEv2 on both peers simplifies re-keying and improves recovery when an endpoint's IP address changes, but you must confirm both sides support IKEv2 before switching.

keyIdea.title: IKE version rule
keyIdea.text: Prefer IKEv2 for new deployments, but ensure both peers use the same IKE version to avoid incompatibility.

content.html:
Comparison›IKEv1 vs IKEv2
IKEv1
Uses main and aggressive mode; main mode hides identities while aggressive mode is faster but less secure. Widely supported but older and more complex.
IKEv2
Streamlined, fewer messages, better NAT traversal, supports MOBIKE for mobility, and generally more reliable and efficient.
Operational note

IKE versions are incompatible. When migrating, verify both peers support IKEv2 and test re-key behavior and NAT traversal settings.

Concrete benefit
IKEv2 reduces negotiation steps, simplifying recovery when an endpoint's IP changes and improving overall reliability.
Key Takeaway

Choose IKEv2 for new deployments, but confirm support and compatibility before migrating.

screens.title: Common Misconfigurations and Errors
screens.subtitle: MM_NO_STATE, mismatched transforms, and proxy-ACL mistakes

narration.text: When an IPsec tunnel fails, there are repeatable patterns to examine. One common debug symptom in IKEv1 is MM_NO_STATE, which typically points to a mismatch during Phase 1 negotiation — for example different encryption, hash, authentication method, or Diffie-Hellman group. Another frequent problem is a mismatched transform-set in Phase 2: if one side insists on AES-256 and the other proposes AES-128, Phase 2 negotiation will fail. Misconfigured crypto ACLs or proxy identities are also common: if the access list that defines 'interesting traffic' does not match on both peers, traffic will not be selected for encryption and will not traverse the tunnel. Finally, forgetting to enable PFS where expected or selecting different DH groups for PFS will prevent SA formation during Phase 2. The practical troubleshooting approach is systematic: first verify IKE versions match, then confirm Phase 1 parameters, next check Phase 2 transforms and PFS, and finally verify ACLs and crypto map bindings. A misconception to avoid is assuming the tunnel failed because of interface issues; often the negotiation layer records the real cause. Takeaway: follow the negotiation sequence and check parameter parity at each phase.

keyIdea.title: Troubleshoot sequence
keyIdea.text: Confirm IKE version, Phase 1 parity, Phase 2 transforms and PFS, then check proxy ACLs and crypto-map bindings.

content.html:
Troubleshooting›Common Errors
MM_NO_STATE and Phase 1
MM_NO_STATE usually indicates Phase 1 negotiation failure. Check that encryption, hash, auth, and DH group match on both peers.
Transform-set mismatches
If Phase 2 fails, verify the transform set matches exactly; AES-256 is not compatible with AES-128 negotiation.
Proxy ACLs

Ensure crypto ACLs match the intended source and destination subnets, otherwise traffic won't be selected for encryption.

Practical checklist
  1. Confirm IKE version parity.
  2. Verify Phase 1 crypto policy.
  3. Verify Phase 2 transform-set and PFS.
  4. Check crypto ACLs and map binding to interface.
Key Takeaway
Work top-down: if Phase 1 fails, Phase 2 cannot succeed; match parameters at every step.

screens.title: Analyze an IPsec Configuration
screens.subtitle: Identify Phase 1 and Phase 2 parameters from a Cisco IOS-XE snippet

narration.text: Let's read a real configuration snippet and map each stanza to Phase 1 or Phase 2 responsibilities. The crypto isakmp policy section defines the IKE Phase 1 policy: encryption, hash, authentication method, Diffie-Hellman group, and lifetime. The crypto ipsec transform-set defines the IPsec transform set used in Phase 2: the ESP encryption and hash algorithms and the mode (tunnel or transport). The crypto map ties these together: it references the peer, the transform set, whether PFS is required, and the access list that matches interesting traffic. From this snippet we can conclude Phase 1 uses AES-256, SHA-384, pre-shared keys, DH group 14, and a 86400-second lifetime. Phase 2 uses ESP with AES-256 and SHA-256-HMAC in tunnel mode. PFS is enabled with group 14. If a peer tried to negotiate AES-128 for Phase 2, the transform-set mismatch would prevent the Phase 2 SA from forming. This is a practical pattern you will use repeatedly: map lines to phases, verify exact algorithm parity, and check ACLs referenced by the crypto map. Analyze an IPsec Configuration means map isakmp policy to phase 1, transform-set to phase 2, and crypto map to the binding and acl that selects traffic.. In practical terms, identify phase 1 and phase 2 parameters from a cisco ios-xe snippet. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Config mapping
keyIdea.text: Map isakmp policy to Phase 1, transform-set to Phase 2, and crypto map to the binding and ACL that selects traffic.

content.html:
Hands-on›Config Walkthrough
Mapping rules
Treat `crypto isakmp policy` as Phase 1, `crypto ipsec transform-set` as Phase 2, and `crypto map` as the binding that references peer, transforms, PFS, and ACLs.
Configuration Snippet
crypto isakmp policy 10
 encryption aes 256
 hash sha384
 authentication pre-share
 group 14
 lifetime 86400

crypto ipsec transform-set MY_TRANSFORM_SET esp-aes 256 esp-sha256-hmac
 mode tunnel

crypto map MY_MAP 10 ipsec-isakmp
 set peer 203.0.113.2
 set transform-set MY_TRANSFORM_SET
 set pfs group 14
 match address 100
Expected analysis

Phase 1: AES-256, SHA-384, pre-shared auth, DH group 14, 86400s. Phase 2: ESP AES-256 with SHA-256-HMAC, tunnel mode, PFS group 14. Transform mismatch with AES-128 would fail Phase 2.

Scenario task
Identify whether PFS is enabled and which group it uses, and predict behavior if a peer proposes AES-128 for Phase 2.
Key Takeaway
Read configs by phase: exact parameter matches determine whether negotiations succeed.

screens.title: Why Choose ESP and Tunnel Mode for Site-to-Site VPNs
screens.subtitle: Security, address hiding, and multi-subnet support

narration.text: ESP in tunnel mode is the standard choice for site-to-site VPNs because it encrypts both the payload and the original IP header, thereby hiding internal addressing and protecting route visibility across the public internet. This is crucial when connecting branch office networks that contain multiple subnets: the full original packet is encapsulated so all internal addresses travel securely inside the tunnel. ESP also offers integrity and authentication so packets cannot be tampered with without detection. A real-world example is a branch office advertising two internal subnets to headquarters over an IPsec tunnel; tunnel mode preserves the original source and destination IP addresses, enabling correct routing at the receiving end. Another benefit is simplifying policy: a single tunnel can carry traffic for many subnets described by crypto ACLs or proxy identities. The trade-offs are additional encapsulation overhead and potential MTU considerations, so ensure path MTU or MSS adjustments are in place. Misconception: believing that GRE by itself provides security—GRE is a tunneling protocol but does not provide encryption, so it is often paired with IPsec ESP for confidentiality. Takeaway: use ESP + tunnel mode for network-to-network privacy and multi-subnet transport, and account for MTU adjustments in deployment planning.

keyIdea.title: Deployment rule
keyIdea.text: ESP + Tunnel mode protects headers and supports multiple subnets, making it ideal for site-to-site VPNs; plan for MTU impact.

content.html:
Real-world›ESP + Tunnel Mode
Why ESP + Tunnel
Encrypts entire original packet so internal IP addresses remain private and multiple subnets can be tunneled through a single IPsec session.
Operational note

Encapsulation increases packet size. Verify MTU/MSS to avoid fragmentation across the tunnel path.

Concrete example
Branch office tunnels two internal subnets to HQ using ESP tunnel mode; HQ routes the received original packets to internal services without exposing addresses to the internet.
Key Takeaway
For site-to-site privacy and multi-subnet support, ESP in tunnel mode is the recommended approach; manage MTU impacts proactively.

screens.title: Key Concepts — What to Remember
screens.subtitle: Three essential concepts from this chapter

narration.text: These three concise concepts capture the most important ideas you should retain. First: Virtual Private Networks create encrypted tunnels that let remote sites and users appear as part of a private network; treat VPNs as transport security that must be combined with internal access controls. Second: IPsec provides integrity, authenticity, confidentiality, and anti-replay through AH and ESP, with ESP being the common choice because it offers encryption. Third: IKE negotiates Security Associations in two phases — Phase 1 secures the IKE channel and Phase 2 negotiates IPsec SAs; mismatched parameters at any phase are the most frequent cause of failed tunnels. Keep these three concepts handy as you read configurations and troubleshoot real deployments.
